title: Solutions development: prioritising, MVP & MMP
blurb: Evaluate and prioritise requirements to reach the optimal solution, and explain how linear and iterative projects do it differently, including MVP and MMP.
question: A meal-kit start-up has 60 requirements for its new ordering app, a fixed budget and investors wanting results within six months. It can't build everything at once. How should the project evaluate and prioritise the requirements, and what should it release first?

teach.body: Solutions development is about evaluating and prioritising the agreed requirements so the project delivers the optimal solution: the one that gives the most benefit within the constraints of time, cost, quality and risk. In plain English: you rarely have the money or time for every wish, so you decide what matters most, compare the ways of delivering it, and build the version that gives the best return. A solution that meets every requirement but arrives late and over budget is not optimal.

teach.h: Typical ways to evaluate and prioritise
items: MoSCoW: sort requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time.
Value versus effort: compare the benefit of each requirement with the work it takes.
Cost-benefit analysis: weigh what a requirement or option costs against the benefits it brings.
Options appraisal: compare alternative solutions (including doing nothing, a partial and a full option) against the business case.

letters.sub: Vital: without it, the solution fails
Important, but the solution still works without it
Desirable, smaller impact if left out: first to drop
Agreed out of this delivery, may return later

teach.caption: The lowercase o's are just there to make it pronounceable. 'W' is 'Won't have THIS TIME', not 'never'.

teach.h: A typical value versus effort grid
teach.caption: Plotting requirements this way makes trade-offs visible to the sponsor and product owner.

teach.h: Reaching the solution: linear vs iterative
teach.caption: Linear suits a bridge, where the design must be right before you build. Iterative suits an app, where users' reactions shape what is worth building.

teach.h: MVP and MMP: the smallest useful steps
teach.body: In iterative life cycles, the solution is delivered in increments. The MINIMUM VIABLE PRODUCT (MVP) is the smallest version that lets you test and learn with real users: does anyone want this, and how do they use it? The MINIMUM MARKETABLE PRODUCT (MMP) is the smallest version with enough value to release to the market or users. The MVP reduces the risk of building the wrong thing; the MMP starts the benefits flowing early.

teach.h: Kitchen Table: from MVP to full solution

steps.label: MVP
steps.sub: Simple web page, orders packed by hand: will people subscribe?

steps.label: Learn
steps.sub: Customers want delivery slots; nobody uses recipe videos

steps.label: MMP
steps.sub: App with ordering, payment and delivery slots: launched

steps.label: Increments
steps.sub: Ratings, loyalty points, added by priority

teach.caption: Learning from the MVP removed a costly feature (recipe videos) before it was built. That is the point of an MVP.

teach.text: Exam traps: an MVP is NOT the first marketable release; it exists to test and learn. The MMP is the smallest version worth releasing. In MoSCoW, 'W' means 'Won't have this time', not 'Would like' or 'Will have later'. And the optimal solution is the best value within constraints, not the one that meets every requirement.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say the aim: the optimal solution delivers the most benefit within time, cost, quality and risk constraints.
Name a technique and how it is used, e.g. MoSCoW, value versus effort, cost-benefit or options appraisal.
Linear: options appraised up front, one solution specified and baselined before build.
Iterative: time and cost fixed, scope prioritised, delivered in increments.
Define MVP (smallest version to test and learn) and MMP (smallest version worth releasing), with a benefit of each.
Optimal solution = most benefit within the constraints, not every requirement.
Prioritise with MoSCoW, value versus effort, cost-benefit and options appraisal.
Linear: appraise options up front, then specify and baseline the full solution.
Iterative: deliver in increments; time and cost fixed, scope flexes.
MVP: smallest version to test and learn. MMP: smallest version worth releasing.

summary: You can now explain how requirements are evaluated and prioritised to reach the optimal solution, using techniques such as MoSCoW and value versus effort. You can also contrast the linear approach with iterative delivery, and explain the difference between an MVP and an MMP and why each is used.

A.q: In MoSCoW prioritisation, what does the 'W' stand for?
A.why: W stands for 'Won't have this time': requirements agreed to be out of the current delivery, which may be reconsidered later.

whyNot.1: 'Would like' is a common misremembering; the category is 'Won't have this time'.
whyNot.2: Nothing in MoSCoW promises a later phase; 'Won't have this time' simply means not now.
whyNot.3: Items worth having if time allows are Could haves.

A.q: Which statement best describes a minimum viable product (MVP)?
options: The smallest version that's good enough to sell
The full product with only the Musts tested
The last release, once all time boxes end
The smallest version used to test and learn
A.why: An MVP is the smallest version that lets the team test assumptions and learn from real users before investing further.

whyNot.0: The smallest version worth releasing to the market is the MMP.
whyNot.1: An MVP is deliberately minimal; it isn't the full product.
whyNot.2: An MVP comes early, not at the end of delivery.

A.q: Which statement best describes the optimal solution?
options: The one meeting every requirement raised
The cheapest option the sponsor will accept
The most benefit within the constraints
The option the delivery team likes best
A.why: The optimal solution gives the best balance of benefit against time, cost, quality and risk: the best value, not the most features.

whyNot.0: Meeting every requirement usually breaks the time or cost constraints and may include low-value items.
whyNot.1: The cheapest option may not deliver the benefits the business case needs.
whyNot.3: The team's preference isn't the test; benefit within constraints is.

B.q: A fitness start-up's app now has class booking, payment and reminders, and the team judges it worth launching to paying members. What is this version best described as?
B.why: The MMP is the smallest version with enough value to release to the market or users, which is exactly this launch.

whyNot.0: An MVP is for testing and learning, not a judged-ready launch to paying customers.
whyNot.2: A PBS is a planning structure listing products, not a release.
whyNot.3: A requirements baseline is the agreed set of requirements, not a product version.

B.q: A transport authority is replacing a road bridge. How will it most likely evaluate the solution options?
options: Appraise them up front, then baseline one
Try each with users in a series of time boxes
Release an MVP bridge and refine it later
Leave the choice open until deployment
B.why: A bridge suits a linear life cycle: options are appraised up front and the chosen solution is fully specified and baselined, because late change is very costly.

whyNot.1: Time-boxed user trials suit iterative work such as software, not structural engineering.
whyNot.2: You can't safely release a partial bridge and learn from it; MVP thinking suits iterative products.
whyNot.3: Leaving the solution open would make design, procurement and safety approval impossible.

B.q: On a typical value versus effort grid, a requirement scores high value and low effort. How should it usually be treated?
B.why: High value for low effort is a quick win: it gives a strong return quickly, so it is normally done early.

whyNot.0: Deferring a high-value, low-effort item wastes easy benefit.
whyNot.1: Low value and high effort items are the ones to drop.
whyNot.2: High value but high effort items are major items needing careful planning.

C.q: Near the end of a time box, the team realises not all the planned items will be finished. Applying MoSCoW, what should it do?
options: Drop Could haves to keep the Must haves
Extend the time box so all items get done
Cut testing so that every feature fits in
Push some Must haves to the next time box
C.why: In iterative delivery time is fixed and scope flexes: lower-priority items (Could haves first) are dropped so the Must haves are delivered to the agreed quality.

whyNot.1: Time boxes are fixed; extending them defeats the approach.
whyNot.2: Quality is protected; cutting testing to squeeze scope in is the wrong trade.
whyNot.3: Must haves are the minimum the increment needs, so they are protected, not pushed out.

C.q: Which TWO statements are correct? 1: An MVP exists mainly to learn from real users. 2: An MMP is the smallest version worth releasing. 3: An MVP must hold every Must have for launch. 4: An MMP always comes before an MVP.
C.why: The MVP tests and learns (1); the MMP is the smallest version with enough value to release (2).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 describes something closer to a launch release; an MVP is deliberately minimal for learning.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 has the order backwards: the MVP normally comes first.

C.q: Why might a sponsor favour iterative delivery with an early MMP, rather than a linear approach, for a new online service?
options: The total scope is fixed and known early
Benefits begin before it is all built
Users only need to be involved at the end
C.why: Releasing an MMP early means benefits start flowing while later increments are still being developed, and user feedback shapes what comes next.

whyNot.0: Fixed, fully known scope is a feature of linear delivery, not iterative.
whyNot.2: Iterative delivery relies on continual prioritisation of changes.
whyNot.3: Iterative delivery needs frequent user involvement, not just at the end.

reteach.title: Think of opening a food stall at a music festival
reteach.question: Two friends want to open a street-food business. How would MoSCoW, an MVP and an MMP help them spend their savings wisely?

blocks.h: Test the recipe before you buy the van
blocks.body: They have a list of dreams: a branded van, ten dishes, card payments, an app. MoSCoW sorts it: a good dish and a way to take payment are Musts; branding is a Should; the app is a Won't have this time. Their MVP is a single dish sold from a borrowed gazebo at one festival: do people buy it, and come back? It sells out, so their MMP is a small trailer with three dishes and card payments: enough to trade every weekend and earn.

blocks.text: Buying the van first is the 'linear' gamble: all the money spent before anyone has tasted the food. The MVP tests the idea cheaply; the MMP is the first version worth trading with.

explain.body: Options appraisal compares alternative ways of meeting the requirements against the business case: their costs, benefits, risks and fit with the constraints. Including a 'do nothing' option gives a baseline to compare the others against, alongside partial and full options.

test.q: In an options appraisal, why is a 'do nothing' option usually included?
options: It is always the cheapest one to approve
It is needed to keep the auditors happy
It avoids having to write a business case
It gives a baseline to compare others to
test.why: Doing nothing shows the cost and consequences of not acting, giving a baseline against which the benefit of every other option can be judged.

whyNot.0: Doing nothing may cost more in the long run, as the problem continues or grows.
whyNot.1: It's included to support a sound decision, not for the auditors' sake.
whyNot.2: Options appraisal is part of building the business case, not a way around it.

explain.body: Must haves are the minimum the solution needs to work. Should haves are important but the solution still works without them. Could haves are desirable with less impact if left out. Won't haves are agreed out of this delivery. In iterative projects, flexing the lower priorities is what lets time and cost stay fixed.

test.q: A requirement is important, but the solution would still work without it. Which MoSCoW category fits best?
test.why: Should haves are important but not vital: the solution still works without them, perhaps with a workaround.

whyNot.0: Must haves are vital: without them the solution fails.
whyNot.2: Could haves are desirable but less important, with a smaller impact if left out.
whyNot.3: Won't have this time items are agreed out of this delivery entirely.

explain.body: An MVP is the smallest version of the solution that lets the team test its assumptions with real users. It reduces the risk of spending heavily on something nobody wants, and its feedback shapes the backlog.

steps.label:
Put it in
front of users

test.q: A charity wants to know if volunteers will actually use a shift-swap app before investing in it. What should it build first?
test.why: An MVP is built to test whether real users want and use the idea before further investment.

whyNot.0: An MMP is a release-ready version; the charity first needs to learn whether the idea works.
whyNot.1: A full baseline commits to detail before the core assumption is tested.
whyNot.3: Costing doesn't answer whether volunteers will use the app.

explain.h: The MMP and the two life cycles
explain.body: The MMP is the smallest version with enough value to release to the market or users. Iterative projects use MVPs and MMPs to deliver value in increments. Linear projects instead appraise options up front and specify and baseline the full solution before building it.

test.q: In which life cycle is the full solution normally specified and baselined before the build starts?
test.why: In a linear life cycle, options are appraised and the full solution is specified and baselined up front, in Definition.

whyNot.0: Iterative life cycles let the solution evolve in increments.
whyNot.1: Evolutionary development is the iterative phase where the solution is built up time box by time box.
whyNot.2: Time-boxed delivery fixes time and lets scope flex, rather than specifying everything first.
